Compare mortality models by penalised log-likelihood

Source: R/compare_models.R
compare_models.Rd

Fits several candidate model()s against one set of experience data and ranks them on penalised log-likelihood, $$L_{\mathrm{P}} = L(\hat\beta) - p, \qquad p = Z^{-1}\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{I}^{-1}).$$ Larger is better. This is Akaike's information criterion without the factor of \(-2\), generalised to an arbitrary log-likelihood weight.

Usage

compare_models(
  exp_data,
  models,
  include = NULL,
  weight = NULL,
  val_relevance = NULL,
  val_distance = NULL,
  test_mortality = default_mortality(),
  Z = NULL,
  settings = NULL,
  overdispersion = NULL,
  time_scale = NULL,
  L_tolerance = default_L_tolerance,
  armijo = default_armijo,
  max_iterations = default_max_iterations,
  max_halvings = default_max_halvings,
  threads = cpp_veil_default_threads()
)

is_model_comparison(x)

best_fit(x)

# S3 method for class 'model_comparison'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary.model_comparison'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'model_comparison'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

exp_data

The experience data.

models

A list of model()s, ideally named. Names appear in the ranking and index fits. A candidate the list does not name takes its model's own name, and one with neither is labelled by position.

include

An include restricting the population, or NULL for all of it.

weight

A pronoun expression for the weight \(w\), or NULL for lives. Weights must not be negative.

val_relevance, val_distance

A pronoun expression for the second weighting factor, in either spelling. At most one may be given.

test_mortality

The mortality on which the \(Z\) scale is measured, once, for every candidate. See fit().

Z

The \(Z\) scale as a single positive number, given instead of a test_mortality rather than as well as one.

settings

A settings() object carrying overdispersion and time_scale.

overdispersion, time_scale

Given directly, these override the settings.

L_tolerance

The convergence tolerance, as a gain in \(L\).

armijo

The fraction of the linearly predicted gain a damped step must actually deliver to be accepted.

max_iterations

The most Newton steps to take.

max_halvings

The most times one step may be halved before a candidate is abandoned.

threads

The number of worker threads.

x, object

A model_comparison.

...

Ignored.

Value

compare_models() returns a model_comparison, whose fields are table (the ranking, best first, with columns L_P, L, p, k and status), fits (the fit of each candidate, in the same order, NULL where one failed), failures (the diagnosis of each failure, named, empty where there were none), Z, overdispersion, population (the population and test-mortality numbers the header reports), arguments (what the comparison was run with, for diagnose()) and labels (what was written for the include, the weight and the test mortality).

table holds the values as computed. print() takes the best candidate's \(L_{\mathrm{P}}\) off both likelihood columns, because differences are what matter and the absolute numbers are large and uninformative – so the winner prints as 0. Both columns shift by the same constant, which keeps \(L - L_{\mathrm{P}} = p\) true row by row.

is_model_comparison() returns a scalar logical.

best_fit() returns the fit of the highest-ranked candidate.

summary() returns a summary.model_comparison: the shifted table as printed, the header's numbers, and in fits the summary() of every converged candidate, best first. Printing it shows the ranking and then each candidate's coefficient table and correlation matrix.

What makes the candidates comparable

Every candidate is fitted over the same data, include, weight, overdispersion and \(Z\), because all of those are arguments of this call and none of them is part of a model. \(Z\) in particular is resolved once and shared: it is measured on test_mortality over this data one time, not once per candidate.

Candidates may differ in their reference mortality. The constant \(\mathrm{A}w\log\mu^{\mathrm{ref}}\) is retained in \(L\), so a comparison across different base tables is meaningful.

Reading the shortfall

Where the weight is absent or is an indicator, \(w^2 = w\) makes \(p\) exactly k, \(L_{\mathrm{P}}\) exactly \(-\)AIC\(/2\), and a shortfall of 1 one parameter's worth – which is the usual threshold for a difference that matters. For an ad hoc weight the penalty is no longer a count and the shortfall carries no such calibration; it still ranks the candidates, but how large a shortfall is worth acting on is a question this function does not answer.

Overdispersion does real work in the ranking. The penalty is free of \(\Omega\) and the fit term is not, so a larger \(\Omega\) favours simpler models, which is the quasi-likelihood behaviour and is why overdispersion is yours to supply.

Examples

data <- exp_data(
  list(
    birth     = datey::datey(c(1945, 1950, 1955, 1940, 1948)),
    male      = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE),
    E2R_start = datey::datey(rep(2015, 5)),
    E2R_end   = datey::datey(c(2020, 2020, 2018, 2020, 2019)),
    E2R_died  = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
  ),
  exp_start = datey::datey(2015),
  exp_end   = datey::datey(2020)
)

# One death of each sex, so the split is identifiable.
reference <- gompertz_mortality()
comparison <- compare_models(
  data,
  models = list(
    level = model(reference, covariates(level = 1)),
    sex   = model(reference, covariates(male = .i$male, female = !.i$male))
  ),
  settings = settings(overdispersion = 1)
)
comparison
#> <model_comparison: 2 candidates, 2 converged>
#>   include         all records
#>   weight          lives
#>   data            2 deaths, 22 years of exposure
#>   test mortality  logmu default
#>                   Aw 2   Ew 0.36215   Ew^2 0.36215   Z 1
#>                   log A/E 1.7088 ± 1.6617 (1 sd) or ± 3.2569 (95%), at overdispersion 1
#>   overdispersion  1
#>   max L_P         -8.862328
#> 
#>          L_P     L     p k
#> level  0.000 1.000 1.000 1
#> sex   -0.985 1.015 2.000 2
coef(best_fit(comparison))
#>    level 
#> 1.708867
